findings.evidence: DOM order is #s3-step3 (style="order:3") "Confirm your order", then #s3-step2 (style="order:2") "Enter payment details", then #s3-step1 (style="order:1") "Choose a plan"; the CSS order values place them visually in the opposite sequence (1, 2, 3).
findings.fix: Reorder the three .step divs in the DOM to match the intended reading sequence (Choose a plan, Enter payment details, Confirm your order) and remove the CSS order overrides, or otherwise make DOM order match visual order.
findings.violation: The DOM order of the three wizard steps is the reverse of the sequence the CSS order property gives them visually, so a linearized or screen-reader reading encounters "Confirm your order" before the plan is chosen or payment is entered, reversing the actual decision sequence WCAG-1.3.2 requires markup order to preserve.

findings.evidence: The only navigation mechanisms anywhere in the document are the header's #nav links ("Plan a trip", "Service alerts") and the footer's #footer-link1 / #footer-link2 ("Privacy policy", "Terms of service"); no search form, sitemap link, or breadcrumb trail appears anywhere.
findings.fix: Add a second independent wayfinding mechanism distinct from #nav, such as a site search form or a breadcrumb trail reflecting this page's place in the site.
findings.violation: WCAG-2.4.5 requires at least two independent ways to locate a page within the site unless the page is one step in a linear process. This is a general rider-updates content page, not a linear-process step, and it exposes exactly one wayfinding mechanism, the primary navigation menu.

findings.evidence: #promo carries aria-invalid="true" with no aria-describedby attribute; the adjacent #s3-form-promo-error span's entire text content is "Error."
findings.fix: Replace "Error." with text naming the actual problem (for example, "Promo code not recognized"), and add aria-describedby="s3-form-promo-error" on #promo so assistive technology announces it when the field receives focus.
findings.violation: The error text accompanying the invalid promo-code field names neither which requirement failed nor what to correct, and is not programmatically associated with the field through aria-describedby, so WCAG-3.3.1's requirement that an error identify the item and describe the problem in text is breached.

findings.evidence: #s3-form-phone-label is styled with style="color:#cc0000"; it is the only one of the form's four labels (#s3-form-topic-label, #s3-form-email-label, #s3-form-phone-label, #s3-form-promo-label) carrying any color styling, with no asterisk, "required" text, or icon alongside it.
findings.fix: Add a visible non-color indicator (such as a "required" suffix or an icon with its own text alternative) alongside or in place of the red styling.
findings.violation: The red color is the sole signal distinguishing this label from its siblings, with no accompanying text or icon carrying the same information, so a color-blind reader cannot perceive what, if anything, is different about the phone field, breaching WCAG-1.4.1.

findings.evidence: #s1-h reads "Accessibility improvements"; the section's paragraphs #s1-p1 and #s1-p2 describe requesting a fare adjustment through the mobile app and checking real-time arrivals by phone, neither of which concerns accessibility.
findings.fix: Retitle the heading to match its actual content (for example, "Fares and real-time arrivals"), or move genuinely accessibility-related content, such as the parking-repainting update already described by #s1-img1's alt text, into this section in place of the fare and arrival paragraphs.
findings.violation: The heading's wording promises a topic that the section's actual paragraph content does not deliver, so a reader scanning headings alone cannot predict what this section covers, breaching WCAG-2.4.6.

findings.evidence: #s2-h reads "Weekend service"; its paragraph #s2-p1 is the same fare-adjustment-request boilerplate as #s1-p1 ("Passengers may request a fare adjustment through the mobile app..."), and the zone-status table #s2-table1 that follows is not weekend-specific either.
findings.fix: Replace the paragraph and table with weekend-specific service information, or rename the heading to match the fare-adjustment content actually present.
findings.violation: The heading names a specific topic, weekend service, that the section's actual content never addresses, breaching WCAG-2.4.6.
